p.x:
We have lots of pets in my house! We have a white rabbit called Snow. She has soft fur and long ears. We also have two goldfish in a big bowl in the living room.
Last month, my aunt gave us a puppy. He is very cute and very naughty. He likes chasing everything, even a little mouse in the garden! Every morning, I brush his fur and give him food.
My best friend has a kitten and a parrot. The parrot can say "Good morning!" and the kitten sleeps all day. Next year, I want to get a hamster too, but my mum says we have enough pets!

Many people want a pet, but owning an animal is a big responsibility. Before you get one, think carefully.
Dogs need a lot of time. They must go for walks on a lead every day, and they need training so that they are obedient. A dog may bark at strangers, but it will also be a loyal companion. Dogs love to fetch balls and lick your face!
Cats are more independent. They like to sleep and purr on your lap, but they may scratch the furniture. Indoor cats need a litter box, which you must clean every day. Make sure your cat wears a collar with your phone number.
All pets need to see a vet regularly. Check your dog's paws and fur for fleas, especially in hot weather. If you go on holiday, you can leave your dog at a kennel.
Sadly, some people abandon their pets when they get bored. This is why there are so many stray dogs and cats in our cities. Why not adopt an animal from a shelter? Some dogs are even trained as guide dogs to help blind people.

Humans have kept animals as companions for thousands of years, but only recently have scientists begun to measure the effects. A growing body of research suggests that pets can benefit both physical and mental health. Dog owners, for instance, tend to walk more and have lower blood pressure, while stroking an affectionate cat can reduce stress hormones.
These findings have led to the rise of therapy animals, which visit hospitals, care homes and schools. Children who read aloud to a calm dog, for example, often gain confidence, perhaps because the animal does not judge them.
However, pet ownership also raises ethical questions. The demand for pedigree animals has encouraged some breeders to prioritise appearance over health, producing dogs with breathing and joint problems. Many vets argue that a healthy mongrel from a shelter is often a better choice. Responsible owners are also encouraged to have their animals neutered, to reduce the number of unwanted litters, and to fit a microchip so that lost pets can be identified.
Even well-meaning owners may not recognise their animals' needs. A dog left alone all day may develop separation anxiety, barking constantly or damaging furniture, while some breeds become territorial and aggressive if not properly socialised. Regular health checks for parasites such as ticks are also essential. In many countries, neglect is now treated as a form of cruelty under the law, reflecting a growing belief that animals have feelings and rights that deserve protection.
